title: Memory Layout of a C Program
html:
A running C program’s address space is split into segments: code, read-only data, initialised data, zero-initialised data (bss), the heap growing up and the stack growing down.

SegmentHoldsLifetimeNotes
Text (.text)Machine code of functionsProgramRead-only + executable; shared between processes
Read-only data (.rodata)String literals, const globalsProgramWriting crashes
Data (.data)Initialised globals / statics (int g = 5;)ProgramValues stored in the executable file
BSS (.bss)Zero / uninitialised globals / staticsProgramOnly the size is stored; zero-filled at load
Heapmalloc / calloc / reallocUntil freeGrows upward; managed by the allocator
StackLocals, parameters, return addressesUntil the function returnsGrows downward; ~8 MB default on Linux/macOS main thread

Inspecting the segments

Stack vs heap

StackHeap
AllocationAutomatic (move the stack pointer)Explicit malloc / free
SpeedVery fastSlower (allocator bookkeeping, possible system call)
SizeSmall, fixed limitLarge — limited by RAM / address space
LifetimeEnds when the function returnsUntil you free it
Failure modeStack overflow (crash)malloc returns NULL; leaks, fragmentation
Typical bugsReturning addresses of locals, huge arrays, deep recursionLeaks, use-after-free, double free

Stack frames

Each call pushes a frame: return address, saved registers, parameters that don’t fit in registers, and locals. Returning pops it — which is exactly why a pointer to a local is dangling after the return.

Watch out

char big[16 * 1024 * 1024]; as a local, or unbounded recursion, overflows the stack. Put large buffers on the heap or make them static.

Where are string literals stored?

In a read-only data segment (.rodata), with static storage duration. Identical literals may share storage. Modifying one is undefined behaviour and usually crashes.

What is the difference between .data and .bss?

Both hold objects with static storage duration. .data holds those with a non-zero initialiser — their initial bytes are stored in the executable. .bss holds zero-initialised ones; the file records only the total size and the loader zero-fills it, keeping executables small.

Why does the stack grow down and the heap grow up?

Historically, so both could share one free region between them and each could grow until they met, without choosing a fixed split in advance. Modern systems use separate mappings with guard pages, but the convention remains on most architectures.
